scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

prediction.raw: As a Christian, my perspective on this scenario is rooted in **love, mutual respect, and biblical principles**—not just personal preference or gender roles. Here’s why I’d give this a **0 (not AITA, but there’s room for growth)**—with a strong emphasis on *how* to handle it biblically and relationally. --- ### **Key Christian Principles at Play:** 1. **Love Covers a Multitude of Sins (1 Peter 4:8)** - Your frustration is understandable, but **love should motivate you to address the issue with patience, not withdrawal**. Refusing to help entirely (even if you’re annoyed) could escalate tension or send the wrong message about teamwork. 2. **Mutual Submission & Serving One Another (Ephesians 5:21, Galatians 5:13)** - Marriage is a **partnership**, not a hierarchy. While you’re right that she shouldn’t expect you to be an expert on everything, **you’re both responsible for the well-being of the relationship and household**. Withdrawing help could feel like a power move, not a selfless one. 3. **Equality in Christ (Galatians 3:28)** - Gender roles in marriage are **complementary, not hierarchical** (Ephesians 5:22-33). While traditional gender norms are outdated, **passivity or helplessness isn’t biblical either**. A woman’s worth isn’t tied to her ability to fix a tire—**but neither is a man’s worth tied to being the sole "fixer."** 4. **Proverbs 14:1 – "The wise woman builds her house..."** - This verse (and its counterpart for men) suggests that **both partners should contribute to the household’s well-being**. If she’s struggling with basic car maintenance, **teaching her (even if she resists) is an act of love**, not control. 5. **Galatians 6:2 – "Carry each other’s burdens"** - You’re carrying some of her burdens (like the tire), but **she’s also carrying emotional burdens (frustration, helplessness) that could be lifted with guidance**. Refusing to engage might make her feel abandoned. --- ### **Why This Isn’t Just About the Tire:** - **Her mindset matters more than the task.** If she believes car maintenance is "a man’s job," she’s likely **passive in other areas too** (e.g., finances, home repairs, personal growth). This can lead to **dependency, resentment, or even spiritual stagnation** (e.g., not trusting God to equip her). - **You’re modeling Christ’s humility (Philippians 2:3-4).** Jesus didn’t withdraw from people’s needs—He met them where they were. **Your refusal to help could feel like rejection**, not just a boundary. - **This could be a test of your patience (James 1:19-20).** If she’s resistant, **how you respond shows her more about your character than your actions ever could**. --- ### **What You *Should* Do (Biblically & Practically):** 1. **Frame it as teamwork, not obligation.** - *"Hey, I don’t want to be the only one who knows how to do this. Let’s figure it out together—maybe I can show you again, or we can find a video we both like. I’d feel better if we both knew how to handle this."* - This shifts from **"You’re failing"** to **"We’re in this together."** 2. **Offer to help *with* her, not *for* her.** - Instead of saying, *"I’ll do it,"* say, *"I’ll go with you to the gas station and help you pump it—then you can practice next time."* - **Action > words.** If she refuses, **go anyway and let her watch**. Sometimes people learn by osmosis. 3. **Address the "Damsel in Distress" narrative gently.** - *"I get that this feels overwhelming, but I don’t want you to ever feel like you *have* to rely on strangers. What if we practiced a few times so you’d feel more confident?"* - Ask her: *"What’s the hardest part about doing this yourself?"* (Fear? Shame? Lack of confidence?) Then address that. 4. **Set a boundary *with* love.** - You’re right that you shouldn’t be expected to be an expert, but **you can say:** *"I’m happy to help you learn, but I’m not going to be your mechanic. If you want to fix this, let’s do it together—I’ll even buy the tools if it helps."* - If she still refuses, **don’t guilt-trip her, but don’t let her guilt-trip you either**. You’ve already shown you’re willing to teach. 5. **Pray for her (and yourself!).** - Ask God to **soften her heart** and give you **patience and wisdom** in how to approach this. Sometimes people resist change because they’re afraid of losing control—or because they’ve been conditioned to expect others to take care of them. 6. **Model what you want to see.** - If she’s passive about car maintenance, **be proactive about other things** (e.g., *"I’ll handle the bills this month—what’s something you’d like to learn to do?"*). This encourages reciprocity. --- ### **Why Refusing Entirely Could Backfire:** - **She might feel abandoned.** If she’s used to relying on you (or others), suddenly not having help could make her feel **insecure or resentful**. - **It reinforces the "man as provider" stereotype she’s rejecting.** Even if you’re tired of being the "fixer," **withdrawing help could make her feel like she’s "failing" as a woman**, which isn’t helpful. - **You might miss a chance to build her up.** Proverbs 12:18 says, *"The words of the reckless pierce like swords, but the tongue of the wise brings healing."* Your frustration could wound her more than the problem itself. --- ### **Final Thought: This Isn’t Just About Cars** This scenario reflects deeper issues: - **Trust:** Does she trust herself to handle things, or does she need external validation (even from strangers)? - **Independence:** Does she see herself as capable, or does she rely on others to define her worth? - **Teamwork:** Does she see marriage as a partnership, or does she expect you to "fix" her problems? **Your role isn’t to be her mechanic—it’s to be her partner, her encourager, and her example of Christ’s love.** That might mean **teaching her, praying for her, or even accepting that she’ll learn at her own pace**—but it shouldn’t mean **withdrawing help entirely**. --- ### **Score: 0 (Not AITA, but there’s a better way)** You’re not wrong for setting boundaries, but **withdrawing all help without addressing the root issue (her mindset) could harm the relationship more than the problem itself**. The goal isn’t to "win" the argument—it’s to **build her up, model Christ-like love, and work *together*** toward a solution. Would you like help crafting a specific way to talk to her about this?
